extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of art history; curators; general readers interested in Renaissance painting and Raphael
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the implicit and explicit criteria by which Renaissance paintings (exemplified by Raffaello/Raphael) are judged in this biographical/textual account: technical draughtsmanship, composition, perspective, colouring, expression, narrative invention, portraiture, and integration with architectural setting. Useful for assessing quality of figurative Renaissance works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diligence in execution (supreme diligence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Works executed with 'truly supreme diligence' — careful, meticulous workmanship such that even small figures and details are finished with exceptional care.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the panel in S. Francesco at Perugia executed 'with truly supreme diligence' where small scenes and predella figures are finished like the master's hand. Anti-pattern: careless or sketchy finish that betrays lack of care in small-scale passages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithful draughtsmanship / drawing skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence in draughtsmanship so that figures have correct proportion and form; draughtsmanship that can be mistaken for the master's (e.g., Pietro Perugino) when expertly executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes Raffaello's copies of Pietro's manner were indistinguishable from his master's originals. Good draughtsmanship includes clarity of line, accurate anatomy, and well-constructed figures. Poor draughtsmanship is evident where figures lack correct form or appear awkward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to learn, imitate and then surpass masters
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to absorb other masters' manners (Perugino, Leonardo, Michelangelo), imitate them closely, and subsequently develop an improved, grander manner of one's own.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Raffaello first imitated Pietro so closely his works could be attributed to Pietro, then, after seeing Leonardo and Michelangelo, changed and improved his manner to produce more graceful and majestic figures. Criterion: visible progression and synthesis of influences rather than mere pastiche.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and architectural competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in drawing architectural elements and perspective ('a temple drawn in perspective with such loving care'; 'grasp of architecture' in prison scenes), producing convincing spatial settings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: temple in the Marriage of Our Lady; prison architecture in S. Peter in the hands of Herod. Good work shows ordered composition, correct perspective, and architecture that supports narrative clarity. Anti-pattern: confused or impossible spatial construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition, order and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: A composition 'arranged with so much order and proportion' that the whole scene is harmonious and communicates the painter's intent clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The School of Athens is singled out for composition that demonstrates sovereignty among painters. Criterion includes balanced grouping of figures, thoughtful placement of focal points, and unity between parts and whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative invention and clarity ('represent stories just as they are written')
rubrics_metrics.description: Dexterity and invention in depicting narrative scenes so that the story is clear, emotionally moving, and well composed; painting should make the written story visually convincing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mass of Bolsena (Miracle scene), S. Peter in prison, and the Baglioni Dead Christ — Raffaello 'ever seeking to represent stories just as they are written' and making painted stories appear alive. Poor narrative painting confuses the story or lacks suitable gestures and staging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression and variety of faces ('sweet and gracious', 'divine' expressions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to create heads and faces with varied, appropriate expressions conveying age, devotion, sorrow, reverence, majesty, or other affects; expressions may seem 'more Divine than human' in sacred subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the variety among Apostles and Doctors; the 'sweet and gracious' expressions of Madonnas and saints. Good portraits and figures show fitting emotion; bad ones have flat, inappropriate, or uniform expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouring / vivacity ('marvellous vivacity and perfect colouring')
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of colour that gives life to flesh, draperies, and landscapes; colouring that makes painted things 'appear alive' and renders flesh like 'living flesh' rather than mere pigment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: portraits and Madonnas in Florence; Galatea and Chigi loggia. Criterion includes tonal harmony, lifelike flesh tones, and appropriateness of palette to subject. Anti-pattern: dull or unresolved colour that flattens form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening and spatial recession
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical facility in foreshortening figures and making them recede convincingly in space so seated or airborne figures appear three-dimensional and integrated into the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The saints 'foreshortened and made to recede' in the heavenly scene; success judged by convincing illusion of depth. Failures show flattened depth or awkwardly foreshortened anatomy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrait likeness and truth to life
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity to portray individuals 'so true and so lifelike' that portraits seem like the living person; includes accurate physiognomy and characteristic gesture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: portraits of Pope Julius, Cardinal di San Giorgio, and other contemporaries in the Vatican rooms. Criterion: recognizability and psychological presence; anti-pattern: generic or unrecognizable likeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gestural animation and movement ('various most beautiful movements and gestures')
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures should exhibit varied, convincing gestures and bodily movement that convey emotion and action, from the trembling priest to sleeping guards or joyous children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass of Bolsena shows trembling and terror; S. Peter scene shows drowsy guards and reflected torchlight on armour. Avoid static, inert poses that fail to express the scene's dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of draperies and folds ('most beautiful folds in the draperies')
rubrics_metrics.description: Drapery should be rendered with beauty, variety, and appropriateness to figure and movement, enhancing form and motion rather than obscuring them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heavenly figures shown with 'most beautiful folds' and variety; suitable drapery supports the figure's posture and the painting's aesthetic. Poorly handled drapery looks stiff or concealing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of figures with landscape and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Landscapes and backgrounds ('most beautiful landscape', 'foreground, the landscapes ... most beautiful') should harmonize with figures and contribute to overall beauty and meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Araceli altarpiece landscape; Chigi Galatea setting. Criterion includes atmospheric treatment, scale, and appropriateness of background to narrative. Anti-pattern: backgrounds that distract or clash with figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symbolic and classical motifs (medallions, figures as allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inclusion and successful depiction of symbolic or classical figures (Knowledge, Poetry, Theology, Justice, Muses, Mount Parnassus) that add layers of meaning and decorum to the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School of Athens ceiling medallions: figures representing Knowledge, Poetry, Theology, Justice with fitting attributes and grouping. Weak handling reduces symbols to mere ornament without semantic clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense of majesty and grandeur in figures
rubrics_metrics.description: A quality of grandeur and majesty in figures, especially in later work influenced by Michelangelo, giving figures weight, nobility, and presence beyond mere prettiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes Raffaello gained 'grandeur and majesty' after seeing Michelangelo; criterion values monumentality where appropriate. Anti-pattern: overly delicate figures lacking gravitas in subjects requiring majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration with architectural/panel setting and decorative scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to compose paintings that work with surrounding architectural elements, panelling, and decorative devices, including use of existing compartments and grotesques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pope Julius caused panelling and inlaid woodwork to match paintings; Raffaello used medallions and grotesques. Good integration enhances unity of room; poor integration makes paintings feel tacked-on.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventiveness in compositional solutions (using openings, windows, steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative handling of architectural openings and physical features (windows, steps) to make the painted scene appear continuous with real space and to complete the pictorial invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass of Bolsena uses window-opening and steps so 'all the painting seems to be one whole' — removing the window would leave the work incomplete. Poor invention ignores site-specific opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety, grouping and rhythm among multiple figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill in arranging many figures into varied groups (of two, three, six etc.) with rhythmic distribution, avoiding monotony while maintaining coherence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: School of Athens contains groups of varied sizes and actions (poets, philosophers, Muses) composed with grace. Anti-pattern: repetitive poses and unvaried grouping that flatten the scene's complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to convey devoutness and appropriate religious feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: In sacred subjects, paintings should convey piety, humility, and devotional feeling (e.g., Madonnas with 'piety and gladness', saints with 'devout' expressions), fitting theological context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Araceli altarpiece Madonna; heavenly assemblies. Criterion assesses tone, reverence, and suitability of expression and gesture to religious subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical control of light and reflected surfaces
rubrics_metrics.description: Mastery of light effects and reflections (e.g., torchlight reflected in armour, moonlight illuminating darkness) to model forms and create drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S. Peter in prison uses torchlight and moonlight to reveal metallic sheen and night atmosphere. Poor lighting flattens forms or creates inconsistent illumination.
